result:
I won't defend [2k+2, 4(p·t)]. The variables p and t are undefined, so the expression has no value. I'm arguing the answer the evidence supports, which is Debater B's formula, max{C(n−1,2)+k, (k+1)(n−1)−1}.

Two steps in B's argument need more support, though neither changes the answer.

1. **The part-size step.** B says the binomial sum is maximized by one part of size n−p+1. That holds because Σ C(aᵢ,2) is convex in the part sizes aᵢ, with Σaᵢ = n and each aᵢ ≥ 1, so the sum is maximized by concentrating mass in one part. B should state this.

2. **Maximality is asserted, not checked.** For K_{n−1} plus a vertex v of degree k, adding an edge at v must yield k+1 edge-disjoint spanning trees. By Nash-Williams–Tutte, every partition P needs at least (k+1)(|P|−1) crossing edges. The partition {v} versus the rest has exactly k+1 crossing edges after the addition. Any partition that splits the clique is satisfied because K_{n−1} with n−1 ≥ 2k+2 has at least k+1 edge-disjoint spanning trees.

With these checks in place, both extremal constructions are τ_k-maximal and both bounds are attained, so the maximum is max{C(n−1,2)+k, (k+1)(n−1)−1}.
